description: Networking from the wire up to the Kubernetes datapath: layering, Ethernet, IP routing, BGP, TCP, DNS, TLS, load balancing, eBPF and triage. For cloud/Kubernetes platform architects who debug real clusters.

notes.text:
OSI model, bottom → top:
L1 {{c1::Physical}}: raw bits on a medium
L2 {{c2::Data Link}}: frames on one link, medium access control (MAC) addressing, error detection
L3 {{c3::Network}}: routing packets end to end across networks
L4 {{c4::Transport}}: process-to-process delivery, reliability
L5 {{c5::Session}}: dialog control
L6 {{c6::Presentation}}: encoding, compression, encryption
L7 {{c7::Application}}: HTTP, DNS, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP)
notes.analogy: Mnemonic bottom-up: Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away.
notes.extra: In practice: people say "layer 4 (L4, transport)" or "layer 7 (L7, application) load balancer" using Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) numbers, even though the internet runs the TCP/IP stack.

notes.text: TCP/IP model, bottom → top: {{c1::Link}} → {{c2::Internet}} (IP, best-effort packet delivery and routing) → {{c3::Transport}} (TCP/User Datagram Protocol (UDP)) → {{c4::Application}}.
notes.extra: vs Open Systems Interconnection (OSI): no separate Session/Presentation layers; apps (or TLS) handle that.

notes.front: Layer 2 (L2, data link) vs layer 3 (L3, network) vs layer 4 (L4, transport): which identifier does each layer use, and how far does it reach?
notes.back:
• L2: medium access control (MAC) address, same segment only
  • L3: IP address, routed across networks
  • L4: port, picks the process on the host
notes.analogy: L2 is the house number on your street, L3 the full postal address, L4 the name on the mailbox inside the building.

notes.front: What does protocol layering buy you?
notes.back: Each layer offers a service to the layer above and uses the layer below through a fixed interface, so one layer's implementation can change (Wi-Fi → fibre) without touching the others.

notes.front: In layered networking, service vs protocol?
notes.back:
Service: operations a layer offers to the layer above (vertical interface).
Protocol: rules for messages exchanged with the peer layer on the other machine (horizontal).

notes.front: What is encapsulation (service data unit (SDU) → protocol data unit (PDU)) as data goes down the stack?
notes.back: Each layer takes the data handed down (SDU) and adds its own header to form its PDU: segment (layer 4 (L4, transport)) → packet (layer 3 (L3, network)) → frame (layer 2 (L2, data link)). The receiver strips headers in reverse.

notes.front: Circuit switching vs packet (store-and-forward) switching?
notes.back:
Circuit: reserves a dedicated path for the whole call; capacity wasted when idle.
Packet: independent packets share links dynamically; efficient but delay varies under load.

notes.text: Delivery modes: {{c1::unicast}} = one receiver; {{c2::multicast}} = a subscribed group; {{c3::broadcast}} = every host on the segment; {{c4::anycast}} = nearest of several hosts sharing one address.

notes.front: LAN vs WAN: what is the defining difference?
notes.back: A local area network (LAN) is privately owned and confined to a building or campus. A wide area network (WAN) spans cities or continents and runs over a carrier's routers and leased lines.

notes.front: Bandwidth vs latency?
notes.back:
Bandwidth: how many bits per second the link carries (width of the pipe).
Latency: how long one bit takes to get across (length of the pipe).
notes.analogy: A motorway: bandwidth is the number of lanes, latency is the drive time. Adding lanes doesn't make the trip shorter.

notes.front: What is the bandwidth-delay product (BDP)?
notes.back: Bandwidth × round-trip time: the amount of data that must be in flight to keep the link full. E.g. 10 Gbit/s × 10 ms = 12.5 MB.
notes.extra: Why it matters: a TCP window smaller than the BDP caps throughput no matter how fat the link is.

notes.text: Nyquist (noiseless channel): max data rate = {{c1::\(2H\log_2 V\)}} bits/s, where H is bandwidth (Hz) and V the number of {{c2::discrete signal levels}}.
Shannon capacity (noisy channel): {{c1::\(C = H\log_2(1 + S/N)\)}} bits/s. More signal levels can't beat it; only more {{c2::bandwidth or signal-to-noise ratio}} can.

notes.front: What is attenuation, and how is it expressed?
notes.back: Loss of signal strength over distance, in dB per unit length. It sets the maximum cable run before a repeater or amplifier is needed.

notes.front: Why are the copper pairs in twisted-pair cable twisted?
notes.back: Twisting makes interference couple equally into both wires, so it cancels at the differential receiver. This reduces crosstalk from neighbouring pairs and outside noise.

notes.front: Cat 5e vs Cat 6/6a twisted pair: what changes in practice?
notes.back: Tighter twists and better separation/shielding allow higher frequencies: Cat 5e ≈ 1 Gbit/s; Cat 6 ≈ 10 Gbit/s up to ~55 m; Cat 6a 10 Gbit/s at 100 m.

notes.front: How does optical fibre carry data?
notes.back: Light pulses travel through a glass core and stay inside by total internal reflection at the core/cladding boundary; light on/off (or phase/amplitude) encodes bits.

notes.front: Multimode vs single-mode fibre: when do you use which?
notes.back:
Multimode: wide core, many light paths that spread out (modal dispersion), cheap optics, ~100–500 m (in-building).
Single-mode: narrow core, one path, km-range links (campus, metro, wide area network (WAN)).

notes.front: GEO vs LEO satellites: why does the orbit matter for networking?
notes.back:
Geostationary Earth orbit (GEO) (~35,800 km) looks stationary, but light needs ~270 ms each way through the satellite.
Low Earth orbit (LEO) (~500–1500 km, e.g. Starlink) gives tens of ms of latency but needs large constellations and handovers.

notes.front: FDM vs TDM multiplexing?
notes.back:
Frequency-division multiplexing (FDM): each signal gets its own frequency band, all transmit at once.
Time-division multiplexing (TDM): each signal gets the full band in turn, in time slots.
notes.analogy: FDM is radio stations on different frequencies; TDM is people taking turns at one microphone.

notes.front: What is WDM (wavelength division multiplexing), and where does it matter?
notes.back: Frequency-division multiplexing (FDM) for light: many wavelengths (colours) carry independent streams on one fibre. Dense wavelength-division multiplexing (DWDM) lets one fibre pair carry many Tbit/s, e.g. for datacenter interconnect.

notes.front: How does CDMA let many transmitters share one band at the same time?
notes.back: In code-division multiple access (CDMA), each sender spreads its bits with a unique, mutually orthogonal chip code; the receiver correlates with one code to extract that sender and the rest looks like noise.
notes.analogy: A party where every pair talks in a different language: you can follow your own conversation and the rest is background noise.

notes.front: Why is asymmetric digital subscriber line (ADSL) asymmetric, and what makes digital subscriber line (DSL) possible on phone lines?
notes.back: DSL uses frequencies above the voice band on the existing copper loop. ADSL gives most of that spectrum to downstream because home users download far more than they upload.

notes.front: What is framing at the data link layer?
notes.back: Splitting the physical layer's bit stream into frames with clear start/end, each with a checksum so the receiver can detect corrupted frames.

notes.text: Framing methods: {{c1::byte count}} in the header; {{c2::flag bytes with byte stuffing}}; {{c3::flag bits with bit stuffing}}; {{c4::physical-layer coding violations}} (e.g. 4B/5B symbols unused for data).

notes.front: What is byte stuffing and why is it needed?
notes.back: When a payload byte equals the flag (or escape) byte, the sender inserts an escape byte before it; the receiver removes it. This stops data from looking like a frame boundary.

notes.front: How does bit stuffing protect the flag pattern 01111110?
notes.back: After five consecutive 1s in the data, the sender inserts a 0; the receiver deletes any 0 that follows five 1s. Data can never contain six 1s in a row.

notes.front: Error-detecting vs error-correcting codes: when do you choose which?
notes.back:
Detecting (cyclic redundancy check (CRC)): cheap, ask for retransmission. Good on reliable links (fibre).
Correcting (Hamming, forward error correction (FEC)): more redundancy, fix errors locally. Good on noisy or long-delay links (wireless, satellite).

notes.front: How does a code's Hamming distance d set what it can do?
notes.back: Hamming distance is the number of differing bits between two codewords. With minimum distance d a code detects up to d−1 bit errors and corrects up to ⌊(d−1)/2⌋.

notes.front: How does a Hamming code correct a single-bit error?
notes.back: Parity bits at power-of-two positions each cover a set of bit positions. The pattern of failing parity checks spells out the binary position of the flipped bit.

notes.front: Cyclic redundancy check (CRC) vs a simple checksum: why does Ethernet use a CRC?
notes.back: A CRC (remainder of polynomial division) catches all burst errors shorter than its length and most others. Simple sums (like the IP/TCP checksum) are cheaper to compute but miss many error patterns.

notes.front: Why is stop-and-wait slow on long links?
notes.back: The sender sends one frame and then waits a full round trip for the acknowledgement (ACK). When the round-trip time (RTT) is much longer than the time to send a frame, the link sits idle most of the time.

notes.front: How big should a sliding window be?
notes.back: Big enough to cover the bandwidth-delay product: window ≥ bandwidth × round-trip time (RTT). Then acknowledgements (ACKs) come back before the window runs out and the pipe stays full.

notes.front: Go-Back-N vs Selective Repeat: what happens after one lost frame?
notes.back:
Go-Back-N: receiver discards later frames; sender resends from the lost one onward. Simple, wastes bandwidth.
Selective Repeat: receiver buffers out-of-order frames; only the lost frame is resent.

notes.front: What is piggybacking?
notes.back: Carrying the acknowledgement (ACK) for received data inside an outgoing data frame in the reverse direction, so no separate ACK frame is needed.

notes.front: What problem does the MAC (Medium Access Control) sublayer solve?
notes.back: Deciding who may transmit next on a shared channel. Static schemes (frequency-division multiplexing (FDM)/time-division multiplexing (TDM)) waste capacity on bursty traffic, so local area networks (LANs) use dynamic, contention-based access.

notes.text: ALOHA: stations send whenever they like. Pure ALOHA peaks at {{c1::~18% (1/2e)}} utilisation; slotted ALOHA doubles this to {{c2::~37% (1/e)}} because sending only at slot starts {{c3::halves the window in which a collision can happen}}.

notes.front: How does CSMA improve on ALOHA?
notes.back: In carrier sense multiple access (CSMA), stations listen first (carrier sense) and transmit only if the channel is idle. Collisions still happen within the propagation delay, but far less often.

notes.text: Carrier sense multiple access (CSMA) variants when the channel is busy: {{c1::1-persistent}} waits and sends the instant it goes idle (collides when several wait); {{c2::non-persistent}} backs off a random time before sensing again; {{c3::p-persistent}} sends with probability p in each idle slot.

notes.front: What does CSMA/CD add, and where was it used?
notes.back: Collision Detection (the CD in carrier sense multiple access with collision detection, CSMA/CD): keep listening while transmitting and abort as soon as a collision is detected, then back off (binary exponential). Used by classic shared-medium Ethernet.

notes.front: Why does modern switched Ethernet not need CSMA/CD?
notes.back: Each full-duplex link joins exactly two devices, with separate send and receive paths. There is no shared collision domain, so collisions can't happen.
notes.extra: Expansion: carrier sense multiple access with collision detection (CSMA/CD)

notes.front: Why does classic Ethernet have a 64-byte minimum frame size?
notes.back: A sender must still be transmitting when news of a collision from the far end of the cable gets back to it. Otherwise it would never know the frame collided.

notes.front: Why does Wi-Fi use carrier sense multiple access with collision avoidance (CSMA/CA) instead of carrier sense multiple access with collision detection (CSMA/CD)?
notes.back: A radio can't hear collisions while it transmits (its own signal swamps the receiver). So 802.11 avoids collisions instead: random backoff, acknowledgement (ACK) for every frame, optional request to send (RTS)/clear to send (CTS).

notes.front: What is the hidden terminal problem, and what mitigates it?
notes.back: A and C can't hear each other, so both sense idle and transmit to B, colliding there. Request to send (RTS)/clear to send (CTS) mitigates it: B's Clear-to-Send is heard by C, which then stays quiet.

notes.front: What is a medium access control (MAC) address and how is it structured?
notes.back: A 48-bit layer 2 (L2, data link) interface address: the first 24 bits are the vendor's organizationally unique identifier (OUI) and the rest is assigned by the vendor. It only matters on the local segment; routers rewrite the L2 header each hop.

notes.front: Hub vs switch vs router?
notes.back:
• Hub (layer 1 (L1, physical)): repeats bits to every port, one collision domain
  • Switch (layer 2 (L2, data link), a multiport bridge): learns medium access control addresses (MACs), forwards frames to one port
  • Router (layer 3 (L3, network)): forwards packets between IP networks, splits broadcast domains

notes.front: What does a virtual local area network (VLAN) do?
notes.back: It splits one physical switch fabric into separate layer 2 (L2, data link) broadcast domains, whatever the port location. 802.1Q tags frames with a 12-bit VLAN ID on trunks. Traffic between VLANs needs a router.

notes.front: Why does a switched local area network (LAN) with redundant links need Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)?
notes.back: Ethernet frames have no time to live (TTL), so a loop makes broadcasts circulate forever (broadcast storm). STP blocks redundant ports to form a loop-free tree and unblocks them on failure.
notes.extra: Modern data centers (DCs): avoid STP with routed leaf-spine (layer 3 (L3, network) to the top-of-rack (ToR) switch) and equal-cost multi-path (ECMP).

notes.front: Datagram vs virtual-circuit network layer?
notes.back:
Datagram (IP): each packet routed independently by destination address, no setup, survives router failure.
Virtual circuit (Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS), Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM)): path set up first, packets carry a short circuit label, state in every router.

notes.front: Routing vs forwarding?
notes.back:
Routing: control plane, computes the tables (Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)), runs in seconds.
Forwarding: data plane, looks up each packet in the table and sends it out a port, runs in nanoseconds.
notes.analogy: Routing is drawing the road map; forwarding is the driver glancing at a signpost at each junction.

notes.front: Static vs adaptive routing: trade-off?
notes.back:
Static: fixed, predictable, no protocol overhead, but doesn't react to failures.
Adaptive (dynamic): reroutes around failures and load, at the cost of protocol traffic and convergence time.

notes.front: What does Dijkstra's algorithm compute in routing, and what does it require?
notes.back: The shortest-path tree from one source to every node, given non-negative link costs. Each link-state router runs it on its copy of the topology.

notes.front: How does distance-vector routing work (e.g. Routing Information Protocol (RIP))?
notes.back: Each router keeps a best-distance and next hop per destination and periodically sends that table to its neighbours (Bellman-Ford). No router sees the full topology.

notes.front: What is count-to-infinity in distance-vector routing?
notes.back: After a link fails, neighbours keep advertising stale routes to each other through the failed path, bumping the metric by 1 each round until it reaches "infinity" (16 in Routing Information Protocol (RIP)). Bad news spreads slowly.

notes.front: How does link-state routing work, and why does it converge faster than distance-vector?
notes.back: Each router floods its link costs to all routers, so everyone holds the full topology map and runs Dijkstra locally. A failure is flooded at once instead of creeping hop by hop.

notes.front: What is Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)?
notes.back: A link-state interior gateway protocol (IGP) for routing inside one autonomous system. It floods link-state advertisements, runs Dijkstra, and supports areas for hierarchy.

notes.front: Why use hierarchical routing (areas, regions, aggregated prefixes)?
notes.back: Routing tables and update floods grow with network size. Grouping routers into regions shrinks both, at the cost of sometimes suboptimal paths.

notes.front: How does a router choose between overlapping routes?
notes.back: Longest prefix match: the most specific prefix wins. 10.1.2.0/24 beats 10.1.0.0/16 beats 10.0.0.0/8. 0.0.0.0/0 wins only when nothing else matches.
notes.analogy: "Netherlands" is a hint, "Utrecht" narrows it, "Oudegracht 12" decides it.
notes.extra: Incident: pod Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) overlaps the corporate network → the more specific route hijacks traffic and "the intranet is unreachable from pods".

notes.front: What service does IP give to the layers above?
notes.back: Connectionless, best-effort datagram delivery: packets may be lost, duplicated, reordered or delayed. Reliability is left to the endpoints (TCP).

notes.text: An Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) address is {{c1::32}} bits (dotted decimal); an Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) address is {{c2::128}} bits (eight groups of hex, :: compresses zeros).

notes.front: Why was Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) created?
notes.back: Mainly Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) address exhaustion: 128-bit addresses remove the need for network address translation (NAT). It also has a simpler fixed header, no router fragmentation and built-in autoconfiguration (stateless address autoconfiguration, SLAAC).

notes.front: What did CIDR change about IP addressing?
notes.back: It replaced fixed class A/B/C sizes with arbitrary prefix lengths (/22). Blocks fit actual needs and contiguous blocks can be aggregated into one route.
notes.extra: Expansion: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)

notes.text: Subnetting borrows host bits for network bits. A /24 holds {{c1::256}} addresses ({{c2::254}} usable hosts); a /26 holds {{c3::64}}; each extra prefix bit {{c4::halves}} the block.
notes.extra: Cloud note: AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet, Azure 5, GCP 4.

notes.front: What does NAT do, and what does it break?
notes.back: It rewrites private source addresses/ports to a shared public IP and tracks the mapping. It breaks end-to-end reachability: inbound connections need port forwarding, and protocols that embed IPs need helpers.
notes.extra: Pitfall: network address translation (NAT) tables expire idle flows, silently killing long-lived quiet TCP connections.

notes.front: What is ICMP used for?
notes.back: Control and error messages for IP: echo request/reply (ping), destination unreachable, time to live (TTL) exceeded (traceroute), and fragmentation needed (Path maximum transmission unit (MTU) Discovery).
notes.extra: Pitfall: blocking all Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) breaks path MTU discovery (PMTUD) and creates MTU black holes.

notes.front: How does Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) resolve an IP to a medium access control (MAC)?
notes.back: Broadcast "who has 10.0.0.5?" on the local segment; the owner replies with its MAC and the answer is cached for a while.
notes.analogy: Shouting "Who is Sam?" across an office; a hand goes up and you remember the face so you don't have to shout again.
notes.extra: Incident: pod IP reused by a new pod but neighbours have the old MAC cached → traffic black-holed until the cache expires. A gratuitous ARP fixes it.

notes.text: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) lease exchange: {{c1::Discover}} → {{c2::Offer}} → {{c3::Request}} → {{c4::Acknowledge}} (DORA). It hands out IP, mask, gateway and DNS servers for a limited lease.

notes.front: What does MPLS do differently from plain IP forwarding?
notes.back: The ingress router assigns a short label; core routers swap labels on a pre-set path (label-switched path (LSP)) instead of doing IP lookups. Main value today: traffic engineering and layer 3 virtual private networks (L3VPNs) for carriers.
notes.extra: Expansion: Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS)

notes.front: What is anycast, and why do DNS resolvers and content delivery networks (CDNs) use it?
notes.back: The same IP prefix is announced from many sites; routing (Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)) delivers each client to the topologically nearest one. You get low latency and automatic failover with no client logic.

notes.front: Why do overlay networks cause maximum transmission unit (MTU) problems?
notes.back: Encapsulation (virtual extensible local area network (VXLAN), Geneve, WireGuard) adds 50–80 bytes. If the pod interface still uses 1500, full-size packets exceed the physical MTU and are dropped or fragmented.
notes.analogy: A letter inside a second envelope: the slot is a fixed size, so the inner letter must be smaller.
notes.extra: Incident: small requests work, large ones hang. Test with ping -M do -s 1400 between pods and lower the container network interface (CNI) MTU.

notes.front: What is a path maximum transmission unit (MTU) discovery (PMTUD) black hole?
notes.back: Path MTU Discovery relies on Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) "fragmentation needed" replies. A firewall that drops ICMP hides the oversized-packet signal, so large packets vanish silently while small ones work.
notes.analogy: A mail room that silently bins oversized envelopes instead of returning them.

notes.front: What does reverse path filtering (rp_filter) do, and how does it break things?
notes.back: In strict mode (1) the kernel drops a packet if the route back to its source wouldn't leave by the interface it arrived on. Asymmetric routing and multi-homed nodes trip it.
notes.analogy: A doorman refusing a parcel because the return address doesn't match the door it came through.
notes.extra: Incident: tcpdump shows traffic arriving, the app never sees it → check net.ipv4.conf.*.rp_filter; use 2 (loose).

notes.front: Flow control vs congestion control?
notes.back:
Flow control: keeps one sender from overrunning one receiver's buffer (TCP receive window (rwnd)).
Congestion control: keeps all senders from overloading the network in between (TCP congestion window (cwnd)).
notes.analogy: Flow control: don't pour faster than the glass can take. Congestion control: don't all flush at once or the building's pipes back up.

notes.front: Leaky bucket vs token bucket?
notes.back:
Leaky bucket: output at a constant rate; bursts are queued or dropped.
Token bucket: tokens accrue at rate r up to depth b; bursts up to b go through at once, the long-run average stays at r.
notes.analogy: Leaky bucket: a drip at a fixed rate. Token bucket: a savings jar; saved-up tokens let you spend a burst.
notes.extra: In practice: API rate limiters and cloud burst credits are token buckets.

notes.front: What does RED (Random Early Detection) do, and why?
notes.back: A router drops (or marks with explicit congestion notification, ECN) packets with rising probability as the average queue grows, before the queue fills. Senders slow down early and one at a time instead of all at once.
notes.extra: Context: avoids synchronized TCP backoff and bufferbloat; modern active queue management (AQM) schemes: CoDel, FQ-CoDel.

notes.front: What is Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) in one sentence?
notes.back: A path-vector protocol in which peers tell each other which prefixes they can reach and via which sequence of autonomous systems (AS_PATH). It runs over TCP 179.
notes.analogy: Word-of-mouth directions: "I can get you to Maple Street, via me then Bob's area." You never see the map, only what neighbours tell you.

notes.front: What is an autonomous system (AS), and why does a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)-peered cluster need an autonomous system number (ASN)?
notes.back: An AS is a set of routers under one routing policy, identified by an ASN. Calico, Cilium or MetalLB peer with the top-of-rack (ToR) switches as their own (private) AS, or share the fabric's AS with internal Border Gateway Protocol (iBGP).

notes.front: IGP vs EGP: what is each for?
notes.back:
Interior gateway protocol (IGP) (Open Shortest Path First (OSPF), Intermediate System to Intermediate System (IS-IS)): fast shortest-path routing inside one autonomous system (AS), optimises metrics.
Exterior gateway protocol (EGP) (Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)): routing between ASes, driven by policy (who you'll carry traffic for), not shortest path.

notes.front: eBGP vs iBGP: what's the practical difference?
notes.back:
External Border Gateway Protocol (eBGP): peers in different autonomous systems (ASes); routes are re-advertised and AS_PATH is prepended.
Internal Border Gateway Protocol (iBGP): same AS; a route learned via iBGP is not passed to another iBGP peer. So iBGP needs a full mesh or a route reflector.
notes.analogy: Gossip rule: you repeat what an outsider told you, but never what a fellow townsperson told you.
notes.extra: Incident: new node's pods unreachable from the fabric → it isn't peered with every node (full mesh) or with the reflector.

notes.front: What is a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) route reflector, and when does a cluster need one?
notes.back: An internal Border Gateway Protocol (iBGP) router allowed to re-advertise iBGP routes to its clients, which removes the full-mesh requirement. Calico defaults to full mesh; at ~50+ nodes switch to reflectors (often the top-of-rack switches, ToRs).
notes.analogy: The town crier: every household tells the crier, and the crier tells everyone.

notes.front: Why would a container network interface (CNI) or MetalLB use Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) instead of an overlay?
notes.back: It advertises pod Classless Inter-Domain Routing ranges (CIDRs) and Service IPs straight into the physical network: no encapsulation, no maximum transmission unit (MTU) loss, and external clients reach pods without a network address translation (NAT) hop. Cost: the network team must accept your peers.
notes.analogy: Registering your street with the city so the post delivers to your door, instead of re-enveloping every letter to a sorting hub.

notes.text: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) best-path order (the parts that matter on-prem): highest {{c1::Weight}} (Cisco-local) → highest {{c2::LOCAL_PREF}} → locally originated → shortest {{c3::AS_PATH}} → lowest origin → lowest {{c4::MED}} → external Border Gateway Protocol (eBGP) over internal Border Gateway Protocol (iBGP) → lowest interior gateway protocol (IGP) metric → lowest router ID.
notes.extra:
Incident: traffic to a Service takes a strange path → AS_PATH prepending or a LOCAL_PREF policy is steering it; show ip bgp <prefix> on the top-of-rack (ToR) switch.
Expansion: multi-exit discriminator (MED)

notes.front: A Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) peer sits in state Active. Good or bad?
notes.back: Bad. Active means "still trying to open the TCP session" (Idle → Connect → Active → OpenSent → OpenConfirm → Established). Likely causes: peer unreachable, wrong peer IP, or TCP 179 filtered.
notes.analogy: Active is you still re-dialling after nobody answered.
notes.extra: Check: calicoctl node status / cilium bgp peers; also the switch's neighbour statement.

notes.front: What happens when a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) hold timer expires?
notes.back: The session drops and all routes from that peer are withdrawn. Defaults: keepalive 60 s, hold 90 s (both sides use the lower value).
notes.analogy: 90 seconds of silence means "hang up and forget everything they ever told you".
notes.extra: Incident: node under CPU pressure starves its BGP daemon → pod Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) vanishes from the fabric for ~90 s, then self-heals.

notes.front: Why pair BFD with Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)?
notes.back: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) sends light hellos (e.g. every 300 ms, 3 misses) and detects a failed link or peer in under a second, tearing BGP down instead of waiting 90 s for the hold timer.
notes.analogy: A heart-rate monitor instead of a nurse who checks in every 90 seconds.

notes.front: How does equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) spread traffic for a Service IP advertised by several nodes?
notes.back: The switch installs every next-hop for the same /32 and hashes each flow's 5-tuple to pick one, so load is balanced per flow. Adding or removing a node rehashes many flows unless the switch has resilient hashing.
notes.analogy: Each car gets one of four equal roads by hashing its licence plate; close a road and many cars are reassigned mid-trip.
notes.extra: Incident: rolling restart of MetalLB speakers resets long-lived TCP connections → ECMP rehash.

notes.front: What is a Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) community used for?
notes.back: A 32-bit tag on a route (e.g. 65000:100) that tells other routers which policy to apply: prefer, don't export, blackhole. Well-known: no-export, no-advertise.

notes.front: Why can a recovered node stay unreachable for minutes after its Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session comes back?
notes.back: Route dampening: the switch penalises a prefix that keeps flapping and suppresses it for a while, even after it stabilises.
notes.extra: Fix: clear ip bgp dampening; find out why the node flapped.

notes.front: MetalLB layer 2 (L2, data link) mode, using Address Resolution Protocol (ARP), vs Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) mode?
notes.back:
L2: one node answers ARP for the IP, so all traffic hits that node; failover takes seconds; no load spreading.
BGP: several nodes advertise, equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) spreads traffic, fast failover, but the switches must cooperate.

notes.front: Why is reliability done at the transport layer on end hosts rather than in the network?
notes.back: The end-to-end argument: only the endpoints can confirm data really arrived intact, and the network is run by others. A simple best-effort core plus smart endpoints scales and evolves better.

notes.front: What identifies one TCP connection on a host?
notes.back: The 5-tuple: protocol, source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. A socket is the app's handle on one end of it.

notes.text: Port numbers are {{c1::16}} bits. {{c2::0–1023}} are well-known ports (need privilege to bind on Linux); Linux picks client ephemeral ports from ip_local_port_range, default {{c3::32768–60999}}.

notes.front: TCP vs UDP: what does each give you?
notes.back:
TCP: connection, reliable in-order byte stream, flow and congestion control.
User Datagram Protocol (UDP): connectionless datagrams with ports and a checksum only; no ordering, no retransmission.

notes.front: When would you pick User Datagram Protocol (UDP) over TCP?
notes.back: When late data is useless or the app wants its own reliability: DNS queries, voice/video, games, telemetry, and protocols like QUIC that build their own transport on top.

notes.front: TCP three-way handshake: the steps, and why three?
notes.back: Synchronize (SYN) → synchronize-acknowledge (SYN-ACK) → acknowledge (ACK). Each side must announce its own initial sequence number and see it acknowledged, which takes three messages.

notes.front: Why does closing a TCP connection take four segments?
notes.back: TCP is full duplex, so each direction closes on its own: finish (FIN) → acknowledgement (ACK) one way, FIN → ACK the other. One side can keep sending after the other has finished (half-close).

notes.front: What are TCP sequence numbers for?
notes.back: They number every byte, so the receiver can reorder segments, discard duplicates, and send cumulative acknowledgements (ACKs) ("I have everything up to byte N").

notes.front: What does the TCP receive window (rwnd) control?
notes.back: Flow control: the receiver advertises how much free buffer it has, and the sender may not have more unacknowledged bytes than that in flight.

notes.front: TCP receive window (rwnd) vs congestion window (cwnd): which limits the sender?
notes.back: The smaller one. rwnd is set by the receiver (buffer space). cwnd is the sender's own estimate of what the network can take. In-flight data ≤ min(rwnd, cwnd).

notes.front: How does TCP set its retransmission timeout (RTO)?
notes.back: From a smoothed round-trip time (RTT) plus four times its measured variance. When the RTO fires, TCP retransmits and doubles the RTO (exponential backoff).

notes.front: What is TCP slow start?
notes.back: Congestion window (cwnd) starts small (~10 segments) and doubles every round-trip time (RTT), one segment per acknowledgement (ACK), until it reaches slow-start threshold (ssthresh) or a loss happens. "Slow" only compared to sending a full window at once.

notes.front: What is AIMD in TCP congestion avoidance?
notes.back: Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease (AIMD): above slow-start threshold (ssthresh), congestion window (cwnd) grows by ~1 segment per round-trip time (RTT), and on loss it is cut (halved in Reno). This makes competing flows converge on a fair share.

notes.front: What do three duplicate acknowledgements (ACKs) trigger in TCP, and why three?
notes.back: Fast retransmit of the missing segment, without waiting for the retransmission timeout (RTO). One or two dup ACKs could just be reordering; three strongly suggests loss.

notes.front: After fast retransmit, why doesn't TCP fall back to slow start (fast recovery)?
notes.back: Dup acknowledgements (ACKs) prove later segments are still getting through, so the path is working. TCP halves congestion window (cwnd) and continues linearly. Only a retransmission timeout (RTO) resets cwnd to 1.

notes.front: What is silly window syndrome?
notes.back: Sender and receiver end up trading tiny segments: the receiver advertises a few bytes of window, or the app writes a byte at a time. Header overhead swamps the payload. Fixes: Nagle (sender), don't advertise small windows (receiver).

notes.front: What does Nagle's algorithm do?
notes.back: While data is unacknowledged, the sender holds back small writes and coalesces them into one segment until the acknowledgement (ACK) arrives or a full segment is ready.
notes.extra: Pitfall: Nagle + delayed ACK can add ~40–200 ms per request for chatty remote procedure calls (RPCs); latency-sensitive apps set TCP_NODELAY.

notes.front: What is TCP head-of-line blocking?
notes.back: One lost segment holds back all later, already-received data from the app until the retransmission arrives, because TCP delivers strictly in order.

notes.front: What does QUIC fix compared with TCP + TLS?
notes.back: It runs over User Datagram Protocol (UDP) with TLS 1.3 built in: a 1 round-trip time (1-RTT) (or 0 round-trip time (0-RTT)) setup, independent streams so one loss doesn't stall the others, and connection migration across IP changes. HTTP/3 runs on it.

notes.front: What is TIME_WAIT and who holds it?
notes.back: The side that closes first keeps the 4-tuple for 2×maximum segment lifetime (MSL) (60 s on Linux), so late packets can't corrupt a new connection that reuses the same tuple.
notes.analogy: Keeping a vacated mailbox locked for a minute so stray letters don't reach the next tenant.
notes.extra: Incident: tens of thousands of TIME_WAIT on a proxy → the proxy closes connections, not the client; use keep-alive.

notes.front: What is a half-open TCP connection?
notes.back: One side has lost the connection (crash, expired network address translation (NAT) entry, load balancer (LB) reboot) but the other still thinks it is open. It only finds out when it next sends and gets a reset (RST) or nothing.
notes.analogy: Talking into a phone after the line went dead; you find out only when you ask a question.

notes.front: How do you detect half-open TCP connections in a connection pool, and what's the catch?
notes.back: Enable TCP keepalive (SO_KEEPALIVE) with a short interval, or validate connections on borrow. Catch: the Linux default tcp_keepalive_time is 7200 s, far too long.
notes.extra: Incident: DB pool hands out dead connections after a network blip.

notes.front: Why does a TCP connect often time out after exactly 63 s?
notes.back: Synchronize (SYN) retries back off 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 s; with tcp_syn_retries=6 the total is 63 s (7 → 127 s). That pattern means packets are being silently dropped; an active reject fails at once with "connection refused".
notes.analogy: Knocking, waiting twice as long each time, and leaving after the sixth knock. A slammed door would have told you at once.

notes.front: How is DNS structured?
notes.back: A distributed, hierarchical database: root zone → top-level domains (TLDs) (.com, .nl) → second-level domains → subdomains. Each zone is delegated to its own authoritative servers via name server (NS) records.

notes.front: Recursive vs iterative DNS query?
notes.back:
Recursive: the server (your resolver) must return the final answer, chasing referrals itself.
Iterative: the server returns its best answer, often a referral ("ask .com's servers"), and the asker continues.
notes.analogy: Recursive: a concierge who books the table for you. Iterative: a series of people who each say "ask them over there".
notes.extra: Typical: stub → recursive resolver (recursive query); resolver → root/top-level domain (TLD)/authoritative (iterative).

notes.text: DNS record types: {{c1::A}} → Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) address; {{c2::AAAA}} → Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) address; {{c3::CNAME}} → alias to another name; {{c4::MX}} → mail server for the domain; {{c5::NS}} → delegates a zone to its name servers.
notes.extra:
Pitfall: a canonical name (CNAME) can't sit at the zone apex; providers offer ALIAS/ANAME for that.
Expansions: mail exchange (MX); name server (NS)

notes.front: What does a DNS record's TTL control, and what's the operational catch?
notes.back: How long resolvers may cache the answer. Long time-to-live values (TTLs) cut load and latency but delay cutovers; lower the TTL well before a migration, because caches keep the old TTL until it runs out.

notes.front: HTTP is stateless. How do web apps keep sessions?
notes.back: Each request stands alone, so the server sets a cookie. The browser sends it back on every later request, carrying a session ID or token.

notes.front: Why do persistent (keep-alive) HTTP connections matter?
notes.back: Reusing one TCP (and TLS) connection for many requests skips a new handshake and slow start each time, which cuts latency a lot.
notes.extra: Pitfall: keep-alive pools meet load balancer (LB) idle timeouts; see the idle-timeout card.

notes.front: What did HTTP/2 change over HTTP/1.1?
notes.back: Binary framing, many concurrent request streams multiplexed over one TCP connection, and header compression (HPACK). This removes HTTP-level head-of-line blocking; TCP-level HOL remains (fixed by HTTP/3).

notes.front: SMTP vs IMAP/POP3?
notes.back:
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) pushes mail: client → server and server → server.
Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP)/Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3) pull mail: a client reads from its mailbox (IMAP keeps it on the server, POP3 downloads).

notes.front: How does a content delivery network (CDN) lower latency and origin load?
notes.back: Edge servers close to users cache content; users are steered to a nearby edge (via DNS or anycast). Hits never travel to the origin.

notes.front: What is peer-to-peer architecture, and its main trade-off?
notes.back: Peers act as both client and server and exchange data directly. Capacity grows with the number of users, but discovery, trust and network address translation (NAT) traversal get harder.

notes.front: What does TLS provide?
notes.back: Confidentiality, integrity and server (optionally client) authentication for a byte stream, usually over TCP. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS.

notes.front: How does the TLS 1.3 handshake finish in one round trip?
notes.back: ClientHello already carries a key share (plus Server Name Indication (SNI), Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN)). ServerHello returns its key share, then the encrypted Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished. Client sends Finished and data flows. TLS 1.2 needed 2 round-trip times (RTTs).
notes.analogy: Each stranger mails half a secret in the first envelope; after one exchange both can build the same key.

notes.front: Asymmetric vs symmetric crypto: what does each do in TLS?
notes.back:
Asymmetric (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (ECDHE), Rivest–Shamir–Adleman (RSA)/Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)): key agreement and identity during the handshake, slow.
Symmetric (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode (AES-GCM), ChaCha20): bulk encryption of the data, fast.
notes.analogy: A padlock anyone can snap shut is used once to agree on a shared house key, which both then use for every door.

notes.front: What is perfect forward secrecy?
notes.back: Session keys come from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman and are thrown away, so stealing the server's long-term key later can't decrypt recorded past traffic. Mandatory in TLS 1.3.
notes.analogy: A fresh key cut for every visit and melted down afterwards; stealing the master key later opens no old doors.

notes.front: What does a TLS client need in its trust store, and what must the server send?
notes.back: The client needs only the root certificate authority (CA). The server must send its leaf plus the intermediates, so the client can check the chain link by link up to the root.
notes.analogy: A passport issued by a municipality under the state's authority: the border guard knows states, so the traveller carries the municipality's letter.
notes.extra: Incident: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority → missing intermediate (openssl s_client -showcerts) or corporate root not in the container image.

notes.front: What does TLS hostname verification check, and what commonly breaks it?
notes.back: The requested name must match a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) on the leaf cert (common name (CN) is ignored). Calling a service by IP or by a short name (svc vs svc.ns.svc.cluster.local) fails unless that SAN is there.
notes.extra: Incident: "works with curl -k, fails in the app" → SAN mismatch, not trust.

notes.front: What is SNI, and why do ingress controllers depend on it?
notes.back: Server Name Indication (SNI): the hostname sent in plaintext in ClientHello, so one IP can serve many certificates. Ingress and layer 4 (L4, transport) proxies pick the cert and route on it. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) encrypts it.
notes.extra: Incident: some clients get the wrong cert → they send no SNI (IP access, old libraries, health checkers) and get the default.

notes.front: What is ALPN used for?
notes.back: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation (ALPN): a TLS extension where the client offers protocols (h2, http/1.1) and the server picks one during the handshake, so HTTP/2 is chosen without an extra round trip.
notes.extra: Incident: gRPC (needs h2) fails through a proxy that negotiates only http/1.1 upstream.

notes.front: What is mutual TLS (mTLS), and what does it give a service mesh?
notes.back: Both sides present and verify certificates. Meshes (Istio, Linkerd) and Cilium issue short-lived per-workload certs, so identity no longer depends on IP address.
notes.extra: Incident: mesh-wide 503s every N hours → cert rotation failing (certificate authority (CA) unreachable, clock skew).

notes.front: TLS termination vs passthrough at a load balancer?
notes.back:
Termination: LB decrypts, so it can route on path/headers, retry and add headers; backends get plaintext or re-encrypted traffic.
Passthrough: LB forwards ciphertext and routes only on Server Name Indication (SNI); end-to-end encryption, no layer 7 (L7, application) features.
notes.analogy: Customs opening the parcel to sort by contents vs forwarding it sealed by the outside label.
notes.extra: Incident: path-based ingress rules "ignored" → the route is passthrough.

notes.front: What is the most common TLS outage, and why does it hit so hard?
notes.back: Certificate expiry. Nothing checks validity until a handshake, so at expiry every new connection fails at once. Watch intermediates and internal certificate authority (CA) roots too, not just leaves.
notes.extra: Practice: export days_until_expiry per endpoint; alert at 14 and 7 days.

notes.front: TLS session resumption vs 0 round-trip time (0-RTT): what's the risk of 0-RTT?
notes.back: Resumption reuses a prior secret via a session ticket to skip the expensive handshake. 0-RTT also sends data in the first flight, but that data can be replayed, so it's only safe for idempotent requests.
notes.analogy: A coat-check ticket skips the queue, but so does a photocopy of it.

notes.front: CRL vs OCSP vs OCSP stapling?
notes.back:
Certificate revocation list (CRL): download the certificate authority's (CA's) signed list of revoked serials.
Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP): ask the CA about one cert.
Stapling: the server attaches a fresh OCSP response, so clients needn't call the CA.
notes.extra: Incident: handshakes suddenly seconds slower → OCSP responder unreachable, clients waiting on the timeout. Most clients soft-fail.

notes.front: handshake failure vs certificate verify failed vs connection reset by peer: what does each point to?
notes.back:
• Handshake failure: protocol/cipher mismatch
  • Verify failed: chain, hostname, expiry or trust store
  • Reset: usually not TLS: firewall, load balancer (LB) idle timeout, crashed backend

notes.front: Layer 4 (L4, transport) vs layer 7 (L7, application) load balancer: what can each do?
notes.back:
L4: balances TCP/User Datagram Protocol (UDP) connections by IP/port; never sees HTTP, keeps TLS end to end, very fast.
L7: terminates HTTP(S), routes on host/path/headers, retries and rewrites, balances per request.
notes.analogy: Sorting parcels by the address label (L4) vs opening each one and reading the letter (L7).

notes.front: Layer 4 (L4, transport) load balancer (LB) forwarding modes: full network address translation (NAT) vs destination network address translation (DNAT)-only vs direct server return (DSR). What does the backend see as the client IP?
notes.back:
• Full NAT: the LB's IP; replies go back via the LB
  • DNAT only: the client IP; replies must route back through the LB
  • DSR: the client IP; replies go straight to the client (backend holds the virtual IP (VIP) on loopback)
notes.analogy: Full NAT: the receptionist relays the whole call. DSR: she gives the caller the direct extension and steps away.
notes.extra: Incident: "all requests come from 10.0.0.1" → source network address translation (SNAT). Fix with DSR, PROXY protocol, or externalTrafficPolicy: Local.

notes.front: What is the PROXY protocol, and how does enabling it break things?
notes.back: A small header a layer 4 (L4, transport) load balancer (LB) adds at the start of the TCP stream, carrying the original client IP/port. If the backend isn't configured to parse it, the header corrupts the first request.
notes.extra: Incident: every request returns "400 Bad Request" right after PROXY protocol is enabled on the LB.

notes.front: Active health checks vs passive outlier detection?
notes.back:
Active: the load balancer (LB) probes each backend on a schedule (/healthz, TCP connect).
Passive: the LB watches real traffic and ejects backends that error or time out (Envoy outlier detection).
notes.extra: Incident: LB says healthy, users get errors → the check hits a trivial endpoint that skips the broken dependency.

notes.front: What is connection draining, and why does a Kubernetes pod need a preStop sleep for it?
notes.back: Draining: stop new connections to a backend but let in-flight ones finish. Endpoint removal reaches load balancers (LBs) and kube-proxy asynchronously, so a short preStop sleep keeps the pod serving until traffic stops arriving.
notes.analogy: Switch off a toll lane's light, then process the cars already queued.
notes.extra: Incident: rolling deploy → burst of 502s; no preStop delay.

notes.front: Why does an idle-timeout mismatch cause connection reset on the first request after a quiet spell?
notes.back: The load balancer (LB) or network address translation (NAT) silently drops idle connections; the client's keep-alive pool still thinks they're open and gets a TCP reset (RST). Rule: client idle timeout < LB idle timeout < backend idle timeout.
notes.analogy: The switchboard hangs up silent lines without telling anyone; you start talking and hear a dial tone.
notes.extra: Example: AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) 60 s, Network Load Balancer (NLB) 350 s, many app servers 75 s; first request fails, retry succeeds.

notes.front: What does consistent hashing (ring hash, Maglev) give a load balancer?
notes.back: Keys (client IP, cookie) map to backends on a hash ring, so adding or removing one backend remaps only ~1/N of keys. Used for session affinity, cache locality and stable mappings across LB nodes.
notes.analogy: Guests seated by surname initial: if one table closes, only its guests move.

notes.front: Why does gRPC / HTTP/2 load-balance badly through a layer 4 (L4, transport) balancer?
notes.back: L4 balances connections, and HTTP/2 multiplexes every request over one long-lived connection. Each client pins to one backend, and new replicas get nothing. Fix: layer 7 (L7, application) (per-stream) balancing, or client-side balancing with MAX_CONNECTION_AGE.
notes.analogy: A tour bus of 50 passengers sent to one ticket counter because it's one vehicle.
notes.extra: Incident: one pod at 90% CPU, replicas idle.

notes.front: What is ephemeral (source network address translation (SNAT)) port exhaustion?
notes.back: Each connection from one SNAT IP to the same destination IP:port needs a unique source port (~28k by default), and TIME_WAIT holds each for 60 s. Heavy egress from many pods to one API runs out.
notes.analogy: 64,000 numbered outgoing-call tickets, each quarantined for a minute after use; on a busy morning calls fail while lines sit free.
notes.extra: Fix: more SNAT IPs, connection reuse (keep-alive), a network address translation (NAT) pool. Check ss -s, conntrack.

notes.front: Ingress controller vs the load balancer in front of it?
notes.back: The external LB (often layer 4 (L4, transport)) gets packets to the nodes. The ingress controller (Envoy, NGINX) is a layer 7 (L7, application) proxy in pods that terminates TLS and routes by host/path. Two failure domains, two sets of timeouts and health checks.

notes.front: What does a container network interface (CNI) plugin do when a pod starts, and what is outside its job?
notes.back: It creates a veth pair, moves one end into the pod's netns as eth0, gets an IP from IP address management (IPAM) and adds host routes. How the host reaches other nodes (overlay, Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), fabric) is not CNI's job.

notes.front: What is a veth pair, and how is it used for pods?
notes.back: Two virtual interfaces joined back to back: a frame sent into one comes out the other. One end is the pod's eth0; the other sits on the host, attached to a bridge or routed.
notes.analogy: A patch cable: cut either end and the pod goes silent.
notes.extra: Incident: pod has an IP but no connectivity → check the host-side veth exists and is UP (ip link).

notes.front: What does virtual extensible local area network (VXLAN) encapsulation look like on the wire?
notes.back: The pod's original layer 2 (L2, data link) frame inside a VXLAN header (VXLAN network identifier (VNI)) → User Datagram Protocol (UDP) dst 4789 → outer IP node→node → outer Ethernet. The physical network sees only node-to-node UDP.
notes.analogy: A shipping container: your parcel keeps its label, the container is addressed dock to dock.
notes.extra: Incident: firewall blocks UDP 4789 → pods on different nodes can't talk; same-node works.

notes.front: What is conntrack, and why does its table fill up?
notes.back: Netfilter's connection-tracking table records each flow (5-tuple + state) so network address translation (NAT) and stateful rules work. Entries live until timeout (TCP established: 5 days by default), capped by nf_conntrack_max.
notes.analogy: A bouncer's clipboard: once it's full, new guests are refused even if the club is empty.
notes.extra: Incident: nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet → random failures under load. Raise the limit, shorten timeouts, look for User Datagram Protocol (UDP)/DNS floods.

notes.front: How does kube-proxy in iptables mode implement a ClusterIP Service?
notes.back: Destination network address translation (DNAT) rules in the nat table rewrite ClusterIP:port to one pod IP:targetPort, picked at random (statistic mode random). conntrack remembers the choice so replies are un-NATed.
notes.analogy: A PO Box: letters are re-stamped with a real street address, and the clerk notes which house got each one so replies can be traced.

notes.front: Why does iptables-based Service load balancing scale badly?
notes.back: Rules are matched linearly, and each Service/endpoint adds rules, so at thousands of Services every packet walks a huge list. Each change rewrites the whole table (seconds). IP Virtual Server (IPVS) and extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) use hash lookups (O(1)).
notes.analogy: A guard who reads the whole rulebook for every car and reprints it whenever a rule changes.
notes.extra: Incident: endpoint updates lag on large clusters; rolling deploys hit dead pods.

notes.front: What is hairpin traffic, and what must be configured for it to work?
notes.back: A pod calls a Service that load-balances back to itself: the packet is rewritten by destination network address translation (DNAT) to its own IP and must re-enter through the same bridge port. It needs hairpin mode on the bridge or source network address translation (SNAT, masquerade).
notes.extra: Incident: a pod reaches every replica of a Service except itself.

notes.front: What does externalTrafficPolicy: Local change compared with Cluster?
notes.back: Local: nodes send only to their own pods and don't apply source network address translation (SNAT), so the pod sees the real client IP; nodes with no local pod fail the load balancer (LB) health check. Cluster: may SNAT and hop to another node, and the client IP is lost.
notes.extra: Trade-off: Local can load pods unevenly.

notes.text: Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) networking hooks, earliest first: {{c1::XDP}} runs in the network interface card (NIC) driver before a socket buffer (skb) exists (fastest, drop/redirect); {{c2::TC}} ingress/egress runs on the skb with full metadata (Cilium on pod veths); {{c3::socket/cgroup}} hooks run at connect()/sendmsg(), before any packet exists.
notes.analogy: XDP is the guard at the front gate, TC the loading dock, socket hooks the clerk who fixes the address before the letter is written.
notes.extra: Expansions: Express Data Path (XDP); traffic control (TC)

notes.front: What is XDP_DROP used for, and why is it so fast?
notes.back: Distributed denial of service (DDoS) mitigation and rate limiting: it drops packets in the driver before the kernel allocates memory for them, at millions of packets per second per core.

notes.front: How does Cilium replace kube-proxy for ClusterIP traffic?
notes.back: A cgroup extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) hook on connect() rewrites ClusterIP:port to a pod IP:port before any packet exists: no destination network address translation (DNAT), no Service conntrack entry, no iptables walk. NodePort uses traffic control (TC)/Express Data Path (XDP) with direct server return (DSR) or source network address translation (SNAT).
notes.analogy: Correcting the address book on your desk so you write the real address from the start, instead of the post office re-stamping every letter.
notes.extra: Gotcha: tcpdump in the pod never shows the ClusterIP; that's expected with socket-level load balancing (socket-LB).

notes.front: Where does Cilium's datapath keep Service backends, policy and conntrack state?
notes.back: In extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) maps: kernel key/value stores (hash, least recently used (LRU), per-CPU) that the agent writes from userspace and the datapath programs read on every packet.
notes.extra: Incident: cilium bpf lb list shows stale backends → map not updated; agent restart repopulates.

notes.front: How do extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) observability tools (Hubble, Pixie) see traffic without sidecars?
notes.back: They attach to tracepoints, kprobes and socket hooks, write small event records into ring buffers, and userspace reads them. No packet copies in the data path; overhead is typically a few percent.

notes.front: Triage: pod-to-pod works on the same node, fails across nodes. Where do you look?
notes.back: The inter-node path: overlay port blocked (virtual extensible local area network (VXLAN) 4789, Geneve 6081, WireGuard 51820), Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) down (no route to the peer's pod Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR)), maximum transmission unit (MTU) mismatch, or the cloud source/dest check dropping pod IPs.

notes.front: Triage: one node's pods are unreachable from outside, but pod-to-pod on that node works. First check?
notes.back: That node's Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) session: Established? Is its pod Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) in the peer's table? Did the top-of-rack (ToR) switch reject it (prefix list, max-prefix limit)? Local traffic doesn't need BGP.
notes.extra: Incident: max-prefix limit hit after adding nodes → only the newest peer is torn down.

notes.front: Triage: ~1–5% of requests fail at random, not tied to any node or pod. Suspects?
notes.back: Per-flow hashing and full tables: conntrack full, equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) rehash, source network address translation (SNAT) port exhaustion, one dead backend still passing a trivial health check, or DNS (User Datagram Protocol (UDP) conntrack, ndots:5 amplification).
notes.analogy: One cashier in twenty is asleep, and customers are assigned at random, so the complaints look random.

notes.front: Triage: nothing changed, yet a whole class of connections fails at the same moment. Suspects?
notes.back: Something time-based expired: a TLS cert (leaf, intermediate or internal certificate authority (CA)), a Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)/IP address management (IPAM) lease, a container network interface (CNI)/load balancer (LB) controller's API token, or Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) held down by dampening after a reboot.
notes.analogy: The building didn't change; the calendar did.

notes.front: Triage: tcpdump on the node shows the packet arriving, but the pod never gets it. Suspects?
notes.back: Between network interface card (NIC) and pod: a NetworkPolicy/extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF)/iptables drop, rp_filter, a missing route to the pod's veth, or a Service IP with no endpoints. Use hubble observe --verdict DROPPED or iptables -L -v counters.
